title: Co-Creating Organizational Change
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that the most effective way to drive organizational change is to co-create it with the team from the very start, rather than designing a change and then selling or promoting it afterward. It uses the aviation-inspired saying 'Don't involve me in the landing if you don't involve me in the takeoff' to frame the importance of early involvement. The piece contends that inviting team members to define the problem or opportunity themselves, before a solution is proposed, builds ownership that overcomes natural resistance to change. It also acknowledges the limits of this approach when a problem has already passed before a leader can engage others. The archivist sees this as a companion piece to other Admired Leadership essays on change management and stakeholder buy-in.
points: Change is best co-created with the team from the moment a problem or opportunity first appears, not after a solution is designed.
Letting team members define the problem themselves builds ownership that formal 'selling' of change cannot replicate.
Involvement shifts the team's focus from debating whether to change to negotiating the pace of change.
The aviation metaphor of takeoff and landing captures why early involvement prevents late-stage resistance.
When a problem has already passed, a leader should still involve the team as early as circumstances allow.
quotes: People naturally resist change and view it as uncomfortable, hard work, and time-consuming.
Instead of promoting the change, the best leaders co-create it with their team members.
Giving others the right to define the problem and its implications creates a sense of ownership that can’t be overstated.
Team members are left to grapple with the pace of making the change rather than the benefits or risks associated with it.
Once a change issue has been even half-baked without involvement from the team, resistance is sure to follow.
Trust the fact that the plane is much easier to land without the winds of discord blowing across the runway.
